summary: A compact temple-and-viewpoint visit: climb a shaded spiral path to a golden chedi above Bangkok’s Old City. Shortlist it for bells, temple roofs and open-air panoramas, especially if you already plan to explore nearby Rattanakosin. It combines a modest physical effort with an active place of worship; allow time to pause rather than treating it as a staircase workout.
whyGo: See Old City roofs and modern towers from the summit terrace, with the gilded chedi close beside you.
The ascent, bells and temple courtyard offer more variety than a viewpoint alone.
bestFor: Travellers wanting a one-hour Old City stop
skipIf: Several hundred stairs or heat would make the climb uncomfortable.
You need guaranteed clear skyline views or step-free access to the summit.
duration: Allow 60–90 minutes including the climb, summit and courtyard; this is a planning estimate.
cost: Budget THB 100 per foreign adult for the Golden Mount climb, plus transport. Two current independent guides agree; the courtyard is reported free. Bring cash and reconfirm the entrance sign.
hours: Reported daily 07:30–19:00; one guide attributes 07:00–19:00 to TAT. Exact last admission and December exceptions are unconfirmed.
bestTime: Early morning for cooler walking or late afternoon for softer light. Arrive well before closing if aiming for sunset.
gettingThere: Near Phan Fa Lilat in the eastern Old City. Independent directions suggest a roughly 5-minute walk from Phan Fa Lilat canal-boat pier or 15–20 minutes from MRT Sam Yot. A taxi is simplest if the walk is unsuitable; travel times depend on traffic.
booking: Ordinary visits appear to be walk-in; no advance booking requirement was established. A guide is optional.
accessibility: The summit requires several hundred steps; sources disagree between 320 and 344. Do not assume wheelchair or stroller access to the viewpoint. Step-free courtyard routes and accessible toilets were not verified.
practicalTips: Cover shoulders and knees; remove shoes where requested in sacred rooms.
Carry water, sun protection and shoes suitable for stairs; pause if heat makes the climb tiring.
Combine with nearby Loha Prasat rather than making a long cross-city journey for this stop alone.
decemberNotes: A December visit can fit comfortably into an Old City morning or late-afternoon outing, but heat remains a consideration. The annual seven-day fair is associated with Loy Krathong, generally November; do not plan a December visit expecting fair stalls or a procession. No December 2026 special programme was verified.
uncertainties: Current fees and hours are supported by independent guides; TAT’s official page did not expose usable details during research.
Last entry, temporary religious closures, lift provision and accessible facilities remain unknown.
